summary: Children solve money and measure problems that weave fractions and decimals together: finding a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 = 80p), subtracting decimal measures of unequal length (2.5 − 0.75 = 1.75 m), and moving between fractions, decimals and units (3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg). Success rests on reading each decimal digit by its place value rather than as two separate whole numbers, keeping units consistent, aligning on the decimal point before subtracting, and connecting 'a fraction of' to division.
misconceptions: Reads money as two whole numbers: '£3.20 = 3 pounds 2 pence', '£3.5 = 3 pounds 5 pence'
Misaligns decimals of unequal length when subtracting (2.5 − 0.75)
Miscomputes a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 ≠ 80p)
Unit slips: 0.3 kg read as 30 g or 3000 g, or gives grams but not the decimal of a kg

activities.title: Split the £3.20 bar: a quarter as division
steps: Take a bar representing £3.20 and split it into four equal parts.
Read what one part is worth and label it (80p / £0.80).
Write the matching calculation: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p.
Check by adding or multiplying back: 80p × 4 = £3.20.
State in your own words why 'a quarter of' means dividing by 4.
activities.insight: Finding a fraction of an amount is a division: a quarter of £3.20 is £3.20 shared into 4 equal parts, which is 80p.

activities.title: Cut the rope: align the point before subtracting
steps: Start with a 2.5 m rope marked on a ruler or number line.
Cut off 0.75 m and predict the remaining length before calculating.
Rewrite 2.5 as 2.50 so both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
Stack 2.50 above 0.75 with the decimal points lined up vertically, then subtract with borrowing.
Read the remaining length (1.75 m) and check it against your prediction on the ruler.
activities.insight: Decimals with different numbers of decimal places must be aligned on the decimal point before subtracting, because columns must match in place value; writing 2.5 as 2.50 is a helpful way to make the empty hundredths column visible.

activities.title: One mass, two notations: 3/10 of 1 kg
steps: Anchor the fact 1 kg = 1000 g, e.g. on a double number line (kg on one side, g on the other).
Express the same mass as a decimal of a kilogram: 300 g = 0.3 kg.
Convert back the other way too: 0.3 kg = 300 g.
Explain why 300 g and 0.3 kg are two notations for the same amount.
activities.insight: A quantity can be written as a fraction, as grams, or as a decimal of a kilogram, and converting fluently in both directions depends on anchoring 1 kg = 1000 g.

activities.title: Read the money by place value
steps: Look at £3.20 and say what each digit is worth: 3 pounds, 2 tenths of a pound, and 0 hundredths of a pound.
State what the 2 is worth in pence (20p, not 2p) and justify it.
Discuss the trap case: does £3.5 mean 3 pounds 5 pence or 3 pounds 50 pence? Explain which is correct and why.
Model an amount with coins and notes to confirm the tenths of a pound are 10p coins.
Repeat for a length: in 2.5 m, the 5 is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm, not 5 cm.
activities.insight: The digit after the decimal point is tenths of the unit, so the 2 in £3.20 is 20p and the 5 in £3.5 is 50p — not a separate whole number of the smaller unit.

activities.title: Quick checks on money, measure and conversion
steps: Answer: what is ¼ of £3.20? (Correct: 80p / £0.80. The traps 8p and 12.8p are wrong.)
Fill the blank: 2.50 − 0.75 = ___ m. (Correct: 1.75 m.)
Match 0.3 kg to its equivalent in grams (300 g).
For each, briefly write the step you used so the method is visible, not just the answer.
activities.insight: These calculations are cleanly checkable, and the wrong options correspond to specific errors (money-as-two-numbers, misalignment, unit slips) worth recognising and avoiding.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Work these out and show your steps. First, what is 1/4 of £3.20? Second, a rope is 2.5 metres long and you cut off 0.75 metres — how much is left? Third, find 3/10 of 1 kilogram, and give the answer both in grams and as a decimal of a kilogram.' Watch the method — especially how they line up 2.5 and 0.75.
